What is your opinion of Prussia and the 2nd German Reich?

I think it was the pinnacle of Germany's history, with a succession of some of its greatest leaders (Friedrich Wilhelm, Friedrich II. "the Great" and Bismarck). It was very conservative and cautious about expanding, only adding what it could safely take and picking its fights, enemies and friends very carefully.

They get a lot of flak for the Kulturkampf, but I think it was the right thing to try to reign in the Catholic church, as it had become obsolete and increasingly turned into a subversive force against the modern nation state.

The reign of Wilhelm II. was a tragedy. He ignored all the diplomatic effort that had been the foundation of the prosperity of the Reich and barged into the Great War with his pants down, with the known results. If the monarchy could have been kept and the Prussian values restored, rather than to have democracy and economic humiliation forcibly imposed, Germany and Europe would probably have been beter off than with the rise of German-style fascism.

I concur to /u/Skyrock that the Imperial period was the glorious apex of our history, and its antecedent in the independent Kingdom of Prussia equally honourable. Prussia's reputation as an historical warmonger is a fiction of the World Wars: in truth Britain or France spent much more of their time at war than Prussia. Even the North American might, if he looks past the hysteria from 1914, discover in Prussia and her eponymous virtues something of a kindred spirit. I have mentioned before that the German Empire had universal suffrage from its beginning, over a decade before Britain.

I disagree with Skyrock in his negative evaluation of William II, however: I find that his actions were generally sound. An alignment towards Russia would soon render Germany the junior partner in such an arrangement, and it is worth the historical notice that Germany in fact won in the Eastern front in 1917; Russia was then a potential power, yes, but not nearly as developed as it could have been. William II held no ill will for Britain, and rather wished to make his own empire her equal. In a sense, William II was the last Romantic monarch, that is the last to feel in the throne's gleaming the high joy completely: even his decision to stand with Austria in the July Crisis was rooted in a conception of loyalty, honesty and integrity placed above personal safety. The Kaiser freely named his own comparison to the ill fated Burgundian house in this. Though the decision can seem foolhardy in retrospect, it was indeed a last great display of principles taking the place before politics, only possible in the world alas since lost.

A lot of North Americans, or Americans rather, are of course of German ancestry. Notably I'm not one of them but there are a lot of Americans of German ancestry that to this day identify with Germany too much for comfort. This had political power in American isolationism during the wars but ultimately the Anglophile elite won out.

Which is to say that of the Anglosphere countries the US is likely to be the one where you encounter the least anti-German sentiment. Americans were even found to rate Germany higher than Israel or France in terms of US allies. I find that suspect but it is what it is.

Wilhelm II. is one where we will strongly disagree on. I never had much love for romanticism in politics, and neither do I think that it was typical for our Prussian tradition. The great leaders of Prussia have always been about stoic Realpolitik, getting results and the most bang for the buck, and willing to do a 180° turn on their principles if it was for the good of the state (such as Bismarck introducing the welfare state in order to quell the socialists, or partially giving in to Carl Peters due to popular demand despite him realizing that African colonies were nothing more than a costly distraction).

Prussians have a real case for being the West's best soldiers. They did a lot with few resources. Uniting Germany though destabilized Europe. I suppose it was inevitable that they did so with a strong France, etc., to contend with but I think being the most logical continental threat to Britain has been shown historically to never work out well for the threatening country. We have seen the results.

In cultural and technical achievements Germany rivals anyone. Political, post-unification Germany has veered from one disaster to another. The most stable was probably the Communist regime.

No electronic devices in the bedroom. Books only, and a reading lamp. Keep a pen and notepad if you have any thoughts or ideas that have to be recorded, like reminders or to do lists. That's it. Sleep hygiene is just as important as regular hygiene for daily health. Make sure the bedside lamp is a soft yellow/red spectrum incandescent bulb, not a blue/white LED bulb, as they mess with your body's circadian rhythms (blue/white light = sunlight = stay awake).

Excellent advice all around. Soft "warm" color temperatures (yellow and red) aid the melatonin production and make you tired. White "cold" color temperatures aid in serotonin production which helps wake you up and also improves your mood. I live in a place where the sun rises and sets at extreme times depending on the season, so I bought some blackout curtains for the summertime and smart lighting that can shift from cool to warm in the evening to help me fall asleep.

Your other point about writing things down is a good one as well. There's evidence that the things we try to hold in memory can keep us awake and weigh on our minds even when we're not actively thinking about them. Your brain considered pen and paper (or even a smartphone todo list app) to be a "trusted memory system" that allows you to offload the things you have to remember into trusted storage so that your subconscious stops dwelling on them when you're trying to relax.

Two years ago I found out about a nonprofit group that provides cakes (putting bakers in touch with families) for seriously/terminally ill children and their siblings here in the US. I signed up for it and have so far made 3 cakes, one for a sibling and 2 for seriously ill kids. Most of these families face serious medical costs and are constantly running back and forth from the hospital so cake planning is the least of their concerns. You get a basic outline of what they are looking for in a cake or sometimes they just let you create something of your own design, how many people the cake needs to serve etc. Note that all costs come out of your own pocket (which for me is fine to help them forget about an illness for a day). You generally get a months notice for when the cake needs to be ready but the nonprofit also lets you know that anything can happen between the day you get the request and the day the cake is due, so you need to prepare yourself to hear the news the child may have passed before that date.

The looks on the kids faces are priceless as are the looks on the parents faces and all the families I have met so far are lovely and we have kept in contact.

For anyone interested in looking to sign up for this, below I will put links. One is for the US nonprofit and another is for those back home in Australia that may want to sign up.
